title: How I plan teaching sequences
author: Jo Castelino
summary: Castelino, a science teacher, explains how she moved from task-driven to content-driven lessons and now plans her explanations around teaching sequences. She defines a good sequence as one in which each step builds toward a central idea using examples and non-examples. Her method is to identify the sequence, write a list of core questions students must answer, and then plan delivery. For the questions she consults the specification, department resources, textbooks and revision guides, and sometimes a colleague with more expertise. She worked the method through surface area to volume ratio in GCSE Biology. For delivery she scripts diagrams that move from simple to sophisticated and plans for misconceptions using examiner reports and an online misconceptions resource.
points: Castelino's turning point was recognising her lessons were task-driven rather than content-driven and refocusing on clear explanation and questioning.
She defines a teaching sequence as a connected set of steps built around a central idea, designed to help novices build schema.
Her core planning step is to write the list of questions students should be able to answer by the end, drawn from specification, textbooks and trusted revision guides.

She scripts explanations moving from concrete to abstract with planned examples and non-examples, and anticipates misconceptions from experience, examiner reports and an online misconceptions resource.
She treats talking to expert colleagues as a powerful way to improve explanations even for sequences already taught.
quotes: It was only after engaging more on Edutwitter that it dawned on me my lessons were task-driven rather than content-driven. Since that realisation, I have been focusing on my explanations, delivery of explanations, and questioning to check for recall and understanding.

In my opinion, a good teaching sequence flows well with each step leading to the next to build a big picture around a central idea. The examples (and non-examples) you use within a teaching sequence are crucial to ensuring your explanation makes sense. Ultimately, the aim of a teaching sequence is to aid our novice learners build their schema so they can make connections between concepts and ideas, and eventually develop expertise.

Once I have identified a teaching sequence (for example surface area to volume ratio in the context of transport in organisms), the next thing I do is to write a list of questions that I want my students to be able to answer by the end. Before I write this list, I do a few things to help me cover all the relevant information required for this teaching sequence.

However, sometimes, even if I have taught a sequence before, I feel there is still scope to improve my explanation. In this case, besides the above sources, I discuss my explanation with someone with more expertise in teaching that sequence. Hearing other ideas and interpretations can be a powerful way to improve one’s own teaching.
I plan what I can say and/or draw to help my students get an answer to each of my core questions. This is a little like a script.
It is important to be aware of potential misconceptions that students may develop. This knowledge of misconceptions could come from experience of teaching and marking assessments on this topic.
